newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian leader says ASEAN must look at security.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian leader says ASEAN must look at security.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations has achieved much in its first 30 years, but regional security concerns still need to be overcome, Indonesian President Suharto said on Friday.
"ASEAN has made substantial strides," Suharto said in a speech to mark the beginning of the 30th anniversary celebrations of the nine-member grouping.
He is the only head of state still in power from the original five Southeast Asian leaders who formed ASEAN in 1967.

"We still have to address many challenges," Suharto said. "We should continue to effectively overcome various security problems that are not only threatening regional stability but also the economic prosperity and economic dynamism we have been enjoying to date."
Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand formed ASEAN in 1967. They were later joined by Brunei and Vietnam, and Burma and Laos were admitted last month.
"With such expanded membership, the strategic role of our organisation becomes more important to sustain peace and security, as well as economic and social cooperation," Suharto said.
A copy of his speech was distributed in advance.
Earlier, the flags of the nine member nations were unfurled at a ceremony at the ASEAN headquarters in Jakarta.
ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh said in an address at the flag-raising that the vision of ASEAN's founding fathers for a grouping of all 10 Southeast Asian nations was near completion.
The admission of Cambodia, delayed following a political crisis in the country in early July, was only a matter of time, he added.
Indonesian political analyst Dewi Fortuna Anwar told Reuters that with its past achievements and the challenges ahead, ASEAN "has crossed its Rubicon".

It now was a regional entity, although strains remained with different political and social systems in the grouping, ranging from military dictatorship, communism and absolute monarchy to varying degrees of democracy.

Political and diplomatic analysts said the immediate challenges facing ASEAN were its handling of the Cambodia crisis and also the effect of its policy of "constructive engagement" in bringing about political change in Burma.

ASEAN foreign ministers have directed three of their members -- Indonesia's Ali Alatas, Prachuab Chaiyasan of Thailand and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines -- to help mediate an end to the Cambodian crisis.

The ministers are due to meet in Singapore next Monday, but it was not clear what further steps they might make in dealing with Cambodian strongman Hun Sen, who precipitated the crisis by ousting coalition partner and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Burma's military rulers have been ostracised by Western powers with the United States taking the lead in imposing economic sanctions to force political change.
ASEAN has rejected the hardline approach, but has to prove that it can bring about change in Rangoon by bringing Burma into the fold, the analysts said.
Another challenge will be the completion of its vision of developing an ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA) by the year 2003, although officials say this is well on track.

"The passing of 30 years is generally regarded as the completion of an entire generation. So today, we stand at a crossroads...the passing of the torch from the old guard to the new," Secretary-General Singh said.
